strengths: Compelling Motivation and Analysis: The authors provide an intuitive and well-illustrated analysis (including t-SNE and toy velocity field visualizations in Figure 4) showing how semantic dispersion and structured latents accelerate the convergence of diffusion models.

Excellent Efficiency Gains: SVG achieves highly competitive generation results on ImageNet 256x256 with significantly fewer training epochs (e.g., 80 epochs vs. 1400 epochs for vanilla DiT/SiT) and fewer sampling steps (e.g., 10 or 25 steps), demonstrating a massive speedup in both training and inference.

Versatile Unified Representation: Unlike standard VAE latents which are purely generative, the SVG latent space preserves the rich downstream task capabilities of DINOv3, achieving excellent results on linear-probing/fine-tuning tasks like ImageNet classification, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and NYUv2 depth estimation.

Detailed Qualitative Analysis: The paper includes a wide range of qualitative visualizations, including zero-shot editing, latent interpolations, and PCA feature maps, showing the clean and structured nature of the SVG latent space.
weaknesses: Lack of Technical Detail on Distribution Alignment: The 'Distribution Alignment' step (which is crucial for maintaining generative performance, as shown in Table 4 where adding the residual without alignment degrades gFID from 6.12 to 9.03) is not mathematically formulated or clearly explained. It is unclear what loss function or mechanism is used to align the residual features with the DINOv3 distribution, which severely impacts clarity and reproducibility.

Ambiguity in Latent Dimensions: Table 5 states that the input dimension for SVG-B, L, and XL is 16 x 16 x 384. If the frozen DINOv3-ViT-S/16 encoder already produces a 384-dimensional feature map, and the residual encoder features are concatenated along the channel dimension, the total dimensionality should exceed 384. It is unclear if there is a projection layer, or what the exact dimension of the residual encoder output is.

Ineffectiveness of Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG): The authors note that CFG is less effective in their framework. Since the latent space is constructed using highly class-discriminative DINO features, the conditional diffusion model might face semantic redundancy when conditioned on class labels. A deeper discussion or analysis of this phenomenon would have been very valuable.

Limited Scale and Scope: The evaluation is restricted to class-conditional generation on ImageNet-1K at 256x256 resolution. The applicability of SVG to text-to-image (T2I) generation at high resolutions (e.g., 512x512 or 1024x1024) remains underexplored.

strengths: Strong Motivation & Analysis: The paper provides a clear and insightful analysis of why traditional VAE latent spaces lead to slow diffusion training, attributing it to semantic entanglement. The toy example and t-SNE visualizations (Figure 4) elegantly demonstrate how semantic dispersion simplifies the velocity field and training dynamics.

Novel and Unified Representation: Unlike previous works that keep the VAE and align its features with VFMs (e.g., REPA, VA-VAE), SVG completely replaces the VAE with a hybrid representation of frozen DINOv3 features and a lightweight residual feature. This provides a unified feature space that works exceptionally well for both generative and discriminative/perceptual downstream tasks (Table 4).

Outstanding Training and Sampling Efficiency: SVG achieves highly competitive generative performance with incredibly few training epochs (e.g., reaching 3.54 FID-50K in only 80 epochs with 25 sampling steps). This represents a massive reduction in the computational resources required to train high-quality latent diffusion models.

Comprehensive Evaluation: The authors perform extensive experiments on ImageNet 256x256, demonstrating favorable scaling properties (Table 2), and showcasing zero-shot editing (Figure 6) and smooth latent interpolations (Figure 8/9).
weaknesses: High-Dimensional Latent Space: The SVG latent space has 384 channels (16 x 16 x 384), which is significantly larger than the standard VAE latent space (16 x 16 x 4). Although the authors argue this does not heavily impact DiT speed due to its larger internal dimensions, predicting a 384-channel target at every diffusion step does increase the computation of the final projection layer and the loss calculation. Further discussion or profiling on GFLOPs/latency of the diffusion forward pass compared to standard DiT would strengthen the paper.

Unclear 'Distribution Alignment' Details: The exact implementation of how the Residual Encoder's output distribution is aligned with the DINOv3 feature distribution (mentioned in Section 3.3 and Table 4) is not clearly mathematically formulated in the main text. Providing the specific objective/loss function used for this alignment in the methodology section would improve clarity and reproducibility.

Limitation in Scope: The evaluation is currently restricted to class-conditional ImageNet generation. It remains to be seen how well SVG scales to large-scale Text-to-Image (T2I) generation, where aligning text prompts with DINO-based features might be more challenging than with CLIP/T5-based spaces. While acknowledged in the future work, this limits the immediate impact of the method on the dominant text-to-image paradigm.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant topic: unifying visual generation with representation learning (perception and understanding) under a single feature space.
The analysis and toy examples (Figure 4) illustrating the effect of semantic dispersion on flow matching/diffusion training are intuitive and well-presented.

The proposed SVG encoder preserves the strong downstream performance of DINOv3 on perception tasks (e.g., classification, semantic segmentation, depth estimation) while enabling pixel-level reconstruction and competitive generative modeling.
The paper provides extensive qualitative samples, interpolation tests, and zero-shot class-conditioned editing results in both the main text and appendix.
weaknesses: Ambiguity in SVG feature dimension and concatenation: DINOv3-ViT-S/16 produces 384-dimensional features. The authors state that the lightweight Residual Encoder's output is concatenated along the channel dimension with the DINO features. However, Table 5 lists the input dimension to the diffusion model as 16x16x384. If they are concatenated, the dimension should exceed 384. If they are projected back to 384, the projection layer and its impact on the DINO feature space are not detailed.

The claim 'Without Variational Autoencoder' is somewhat misleading: While the authors do not use a standard VAE (with KL divergence or vector quantization), they still construct and train an Autoencoder (frozen DINO + trained Residual Encoder + SVG Decoder) using reconstruction losses. In essence, the standard VAE bottleneck is replaced by an AE bottleneck. Therefore, the core paradigm remains an Autoencoder-based Latent Diffusion Model rather than a truly 'VAE-free' approach (e.g., pixel-space or direct representation generation without decoder training).

Marginal improvement over existing representation-alignment baselines: SVG-XL is heavily compared against SiT-XL. However, when compared to representation-aligned models such as SiT-XL (VA-VAE) in Table 1, the performance gain is quite modest (e.g., at 80 epochs w/ CFG, gFID of 3.54 vs. 4.13). Furthermore, REPA-XL (which also aligns features with a VFM) achieves a superior gFID of 1.42 at 800 epochs, whereas SVG-XL achieves 1.92 gFID at 1400 epochs, despite SVG using the more advanced DINOv3.

Reduced effectiveness of Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG): The authors note in the limitations section that CFG is less effective in their framework. Given how crucial CFG is for text-to-image generation quality, this is a significant limitation of the proposed latent space.

Limited evaluation scope: The generative experiments are conducted solely on ImageNet 256x256 class-conditional generation. Evaluative benchmarks on more complex datasets or large-scale text-to-image (T2I) tasks are missing, which limits the verification of the 'task-general' claim.

strengths: Compelling Motivation & Insightful Analysis: The paper presents a thorough analysis of VAE latent spaces, highlighting how 'semantic entanglement' hampers the training and inference efficiency of latent diffusion models. The t-SNE visualizations and the toy velocity-field example beautifully illustrate the advantage of a semantically discriminative latent space.

Elegant & Lightweight Method (SVG): Directly utilizing frozen self-supervised DINOv3 representations as the core of the latent space, complemented by a lightweight residual encoder, is simple yet powerful. The proposed distribution alignment is highly effective in preserving DINO's semantic structure while integrating fine-grained perceptual details.

Impressive Performance and Efficiency: SVG-XL achieves highly competitive FID scores in a fraction of the training epochs compared to vanilla VAE-based models (e.g., gFID of 3.54 with only 80 training epochs). Furthermore, operating on the structured SVG latent space enables excellent generation quality with very few sampling steps (e.g., 25, 10, or even 5 steps), significantly outperforming baseline models under low NFEs.

Unified Representation: The paper demonstrates that the SVG feature space retains the strong semantic understanding and dense prediction capabilities of DINOv3 on downstream tasks (classification, segmentation, depth estimation), taking a solid step toward unified visual representations.

Comprehensive Evaluation: The paper provides extensive experiments, including scaling behavior, qualitative results (generation, zero-shot editing, linear/spherical interpolations), and detailed ablation studies.
weaknesses: Clarification on Latent Dimensions: The text states that the DINOv3-ViT-S/16 encoder produces a 16x16x384 feature map and that the Residual Encoder's outputs are concatenated along the channel dimension. However, Table 5 lists the 'Input dim.' of SVG-B, SVG-L, and SVG-XL as 16x16x384. If the original DINOv3 feature dimension is already 384, and it is concatenated with the residual feature, the total dimension of the SVG latent space should be larger than 384. It is unclear if there is a projection layer used before concatenation, or if the actual latent dimension input to the diffusion model is larger than 384.

Deeper Discussion on Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG): The authors note in the limitations that CFG is less effective in their framework compared to others. It would be valuable to discuss why this is the case. For instance, is it because the self-supervised features (DINOv3) already contain highly discriminative semantic information, which implicitly guides the diffusion process even without CFG, thereby diminishing the relative gain from explicit class conditioning?

Missing Comparison/Discussion with Representation-Conditioned Generation (RCG): RCG (e.g., Li et al., 'Return of Unconditional Generation', NeurIPS 2023) is a highly relevant paradigm that also leverages self-supervised representations for image generation. Although RCG uses a two-stage generation process (generating representations first, then decoding/generating pixels conditioned on them), a discussion on how SVG differs from or improves upon RCG-style frameworks would provide better context.

Minor Note on Terminology: The title 'Latent Diffusion Model without Variational Autoencoder' might initially lead some readers to think the model operates directly in pixel space. Since SVG still uses an autoencoder (comprising DINO + Residual Encoder + SVG Decoder) without the variational (KL) constraint, the model is a latent diffusion model with a standard Autoencoder. A brief note clarifying this helps prevent any initial misunderstanding.

strengths: Strong motivation and intuitive theoretical justification: The paper provides a compelling analysis using t-SNE visualizations and a toy velocity field model to demonstrate how semantic entanglement in standard VAE latent spaces slows down diffusion training and impairs few-step sampling.

Remarkable training and inference efficiency: By leveraging semantically structured latents, SVG achieves competitive ImageNet 256x256 generation results in significantly fewer epochs (e.g., 80 to 500 epochs) compared to traditional VAE-based models that require 1400+ epochs, while excelling in few-step generation (5-25 steps).

Preservation of downstream task generalizability: Unlike purely generative latents, the SVG representation retains the rich discriminative capabilities of DINO features, performing well on dense prediction and classification tasks (Table 4).

Detailed empirical evaluation: The paper contains extensive experiments, including encoder feature space comparisons, model scaling, visual editing, and latent interpolations, accompanied by a large volume of uncurated qualitative results.
weaknesses: Clarity issue regarding feature dimensions and concatenation: The text states that the DINOv3-ViT-S/16 encoder produces a 16x16x384 feature map and that the Residual Encoder's outputs are concatenated to form the complete SVG feature. However, Table 5 lists the input dimension of the diffusion model as 16x16x384. If the two features are concatenated, the total dimension should be larger than 384. The authors need to clarify the exact dimensionality of the residual features and the final concatenated SVG latent space.

Trade-off in reconstruction fidelity: The reconstruction FID (rFID) of SVGTok is 0.65, which is notably worse than VA-VAE's rFID of 0.26 (Table 1). This indicates that the proposed method sacrifices some fine-grained reconstruction fidelity to maintain semantic structure and training speed. This trade-off should be explicitly discussed.

Dependency on DINOv3: The paper relies heavily on DINOv3, which is an extremely recent model. It remains unclear how easily reproducible the results are if DINOv3 weights are not fully accessible to the general community. Demonstrating the performance with more widely available models (e.g., DINOv2 or SigLIP) in the main pipeline would increase the paper's impact and reproducibility.

Slightly misleading 'Without Variational Autoencoder' terminology: While the model avoids using a variational autoencoder (VAE with KL-divergence), it still trains and relies on a customized autoencoding pipeline (SVG Autoencoder) with a decoder to map the latent representation back to pixels. This is conceptually very similar to standard Autoencoder-based latent diffusion (e.g., VQ-GAN or AE with weak regularization), which makes the title's claim sound slightly overstated.

strengths: The paper presents a highly compelling concept of using a semantically structured latent space derived from self-supervised vision foundation models (specifically DINOv3) instead of traditional variational autoencoders (VAEs).

Comprehensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed SVG model converges substantially faster during training and achieves excellent generation quality (gFID of 1.92 on ImageNet 256x256) with very few sampling steps (e.g., 25 Euler steps).
The paper provides a thorough analysis and visualization of the semantic dispersion of the latent space, explaining why a structured latent space benefits flow matching and diffusion optimization.

Unlike VAE-based models, the SVG latent space retains strong downstream performance on perception and understanding tasks (like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation), showing its promise as a unified representation.
Extensive qualitative results, including uncurated samples across various classes, demonstrate the robustness and diversity of the generation.
weaknesses: There is a minor lack of clarity regarding the channel dimensions of the SVG latent space. If DINOv3-ViT-S/16 produces $16 \times 16 \times 384$ features, and the residual encoder outputs are concatenated along the channel dimension, the total channel dimension should exceed 384. However, Table 5 lists the input dimension as $16 \times 16 \times 384$. The authors should clarify if any projection is applied to the features.

The framework seems to suffer from a degradation in classifier-free guidance (CFG) effectiveness at higher scales, as shown in Figure 13 and discussed in the limitations. Standard diffusion models typically benefit from larger CFG scales, whereas SVG's performance peaks at lower scales.

While the title highlights being 'without Variational Autoencoder', the model still heavily relies on an encoder-decoder architecture (the SVG Autoencoder) with reconstruction losses. The core change is the omission of the variational/KL bottleneck and the incorporation of frozen VFM features, rather than completely removing the autoencoder-style abstraction.

The experimental evaluation is restricted to class-conditional ImageNet generation. Extending the method to text-to-image or text-to-video generation would make the evaluation much stronger and show its generalizability.
